evidence.excerpt: This study used a participatory design and evaluation approach to assess the cognitive accessibility of a mobile application for hypertension self-management intended for use by patients with low health literacy. Thirty adults attending a hypertension clinic were recruited; 60% had primary or lower-secondary education and scored in the lowest two quintiles of the SRI-based health literacy screener. Three participatory workshops were conducted in which participants attempted core app tasks (recording blood pressure, interpreting trend graphs, reading medication reminders) with a researcher observing and probing. Usability problems were classified using a structured error taxonomy. Trend graph interpretation was the most problematic feature, with 73% of low-literacy participants misreading directionality on inverted axes. Written medication reminders averaging 24 words per notification produced substantially higher error rates than reminders of 10 words or fewer. A revised prototype incorporating plain-text notifications and simplified graphs was tested in a second round with 18 participants and showed a 44% reduction in task-error rate.
